title: SRE abuse response playbook — traffic floods & WAF tuning (draft)
executive_summary: Draft playbook for on-call and post-incident follow-up for high-rate-abuse incidents (traffic floods, stolen API keys, WAF bypass attempts). Focus areas: immediate containment, meter-based throttling changes, temporary rule pushes to WAF, KMS/key rotation coordination, and short-term telemetry to validate containment.
content:
Context:
This doc collects practical, battle-tested actions and notes from several recent incidents where abusive traffic overwhelmed endpoints or exploited leaked API keys. It's intentionally pragmatic — prioritizes things an on-call SRE can do in the first 60–180 minutes, plus a set of follow-ups for engineering and product.

Goals for on-call:
- Quickly reduce user-facing errors and latency spikes
- Stop or drastically reduce abusive traffic volume
- Preserve legitimate customer traffic when possible
- Gather artifacts for post-incident analysis

Scope of incidents covered:
- Large volumetric request floods (bots, misconfigured clients) against public API and streaming endpoints
- Credential leakage (API keys found in public repos or exposed in telemetry) leading to high-usage keys
- Application-layer abuse attempts where WAF rules are required (SQLi, path traversal, suspicious payloads)

Immediate indicators (what you will see)
- Sudden spike in 5xx errors and tail latency on /v1/generate or internal inference routes
- Token/compute saturation alerts from serving-runtime metrics (GPU queue length, OOMs)
- Rate limiter logs showing many distinct API keys with high rates or one key with huge RPS
- WAF console showing repetitive block/allow patterns or high rule firing counts

Incident timeline template (use for notes)
- T+0m: Alert triggered — who acknowledged (on-call)
- T+5m: Quick triage — source IP clusters, top API keys, affected endpoints
- T+15m: Containment actions taken (details below)
- T+30–60m: Confirm reduction in error rate and latency; gather logs for postmortem
- T+3h: Escalation to product/security if keys/data exfiltration suspected

Runbook — Quick containment actions (first 0–30 minutes)
1) Throttle aggressive consumers fast:
   - Apply emergency rate limit overrides at the edge for the affected route(s): drop burst to 50 rps per IP and 10 rps per key as a temporary measure.
   - If traffic is from many IPs but a small set of keys: throttle by key first. If many keys, fallback to IP/subnet or geo-based throttles.
2) Promote fail-open vs fail-closed decisions sparingly:
   - For critical internal customer endpoints, prefer graceful degradation (reject heavy features) rather than full blocking.
3) Emergency WAF rules:
   - Push a narrow, temporary WAF rule to block the most obvious request patterns (user-agent string, path regex, specific header patterns). Keep TTL short (60–120m) and annotate rule with author and reason.
4) Key revocation for compromised keys:
   - If logs show a small number of keys producing the majority of abusive traffic, revoke those keys immediately and rotate. Notify CS for customer-facing communications.
5) Autoscale / capacity reactions:
   - If burst is transient and legitimate, ramping capacity may be cheaper/faster than blocking. Coordinate with infra and release_engineering if GPU provisioning is needed.

Evidence collection (parallel to containment)
- Snapshot ingress flow logs for the time range and export top 100 source IPs and keys.
- Collect WAF rule hits, raw request bodies (if not PII), and X-Request-IDs.
- Save serving-runtime traces for affected requests (kv-cache sizes, batch sizes).

Medium-term actions (30m–6h)
- Replace emergency WAF rules with more precise rules after analysis.
- Implement per-customer or per-key hard quotas if abuse is targeted.
- If keys were leaked: rotate keys, audit last-seen IPs, add Geo IP blocks or step-up auth for the customer if available.
- Add temporary telemetry dashboards showing key-heavy traffic and error rates.

WAF tuning notes (practical tips)
- Start with deny-by-pattern that has a high precision: specific payload regex, exact user-agent, or header fingerprinting. Avoid generic heuristics that will hit false positives.
- Use rate-based WAF rules only when you can scope them (per route or per key) to avoid collateral damage.
- Tag every emergency WAF rule with: author, reason, start_time, expected_expiry. Have an automated cleanup that expires temp rules.

Rate limiter configuration guidance
- Two-layer approach: global token-bucket at edge + per-key shaped quotas in API gateway.
- For sudden floods, prefer steep penalty backoff: 429 + Retry-After progressive backoff.
- Quota escalation: if a key exceeds X tokens/min for 3 continuous minutes, automatically reduce allowed concurrency by Y%.
- Keep a fast-extract top-n keys routine in control plane to identify top offenders without scanning logs.

Key-leak specific steps
- If a key appears in public repo or security feed: immediately revoke and issue new key.
- Run a search across telemetry for first-seen timestamp and IPs used. Mark those IPs for short-term stricter throttling.
- Notify legal/infosec if PII or customer data requests are suspected.

On-call playbook (concise checklist)
- Acknowledge alert and set up incident channel (Slack + Zoom)
- Snapshot metrics and flow logs
- Apply emergency throttles (key -> IP -> geo order)
- Push precise WAF rules with expiry
- Revoke compromised keys and start rotation workflow
- Communicate to CS/PM about potential customer impact
- Keep notes and mark times for postmortem timeline

Monitoring & alerting to add after incident
- Alert on unusual key-skew: top-5 keys consuming > 40% of requests in 10m window
- Alert on sudden rise in WAF rule hits by > 200% over baseline
- SLO guardrails: notify when error budget consumption accelerates beyond planned thresholds

Post-incident action items (examples)
- Short-term (within 72h): automate temp-WAF TTLs, add quick revoke path for keys with one-click rotation UI, add dashboard for key-skew metric (owner: infra/edge).
- Medium-term (2–6 weeks): build per-key hard quotas and automated mitigations, evaluate more fingerprinting data to reduce false positives (owner: serving-runtime + eng-sre).
- Long-term (quarterly): integrate key usage analytics into billing/alerting to detect early anomalies; refine SDKs to reduce accidental token leakage (owner: developer-experience).

Runbook validation checklist
- Practise tabletop once a quarter with simulated key-leak and traffic flood scenarios.
- Validate WAF push and revert automation in staging.
- Ensure CS and legal have playbooks for customer notification and compliance reporting.

Notes from recent incidents (scratchpad)
- 2024-09-21: Botnet-style flood hit /v1/chat/streaming. Emergency rule based on "X-Client-Id" header pattern dropped volume by 70% in 12m. False positive rate after revert: ~1.2% (users with older SDKs). Ticket: SRE-3980.
- 2024-10-18: Single leaked key from partner integration accounted for 82% of anomalous traffic. Immediate revoke + rotation solved after 9m; but we lacked one-click rotation for partners (action: devexp-124).

Open questions / unresolved tradeoffs
- Thresholds: what are safe default emergency throttle values that work across hosted and dedicated customers? (product/legal input needed).
- Communication: when do we inform affected customers vs when to quietly mitigate? (policy required).
- Autoscale vs block: need clearer cost thresholds for choosing to auto-scale GPUs vs apply aggressive limits.

Immediate TODOs (owner assignments)
- (Liam) implement temp-WAF TTL automation and cleanup job — due 2024-12-16
- (Ritika) build dashboard for top-key skew and alerting — due 2024-12-09
- (Omar) add one-click key rotation flow in partner console (design doc draft) — due 2025-01-15

Appendix: Useful commands & locations
- Edge rule push: infra/edge CLI command: infra-edge rules push --file tmp-rule.json --env prod --ttl 60m
- Query logs: kubectl logs -l app=api-gateway --since=30m | jq '.request.key' | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -n 50
- WAF console: https://waf-console.internal.redwood.company/rules
- Incident ticket template: https://jira.redwood.company/browse/SRE-INCIDENT-TEMPLATE

End of draft. Please add notes, test playbook in staging, and iterate.
incident_timeline: T+0: pagerduty alert fired for 5xx spike and GPU queue length; T+3m: SRE on-call acknowledged (Maya); T+8m: identified small set of keys with extreme RPS; T+12m: emergency throttle by key applied; T+18m: temp WAF rule to block UA pattern pushed; T+28m: error rate reduced 65%; T+2h: post-containment analysis started; T+6h: rotated 4 compromised keys; T+24h: customer comms drafted for impacted partners.
runbook_quick_actions: 1) Snapshot metrics and logs; 2) Apply per-key throttle; 3) If high-IP-vol, apply geo/IP throttle; 4) Push temp WAF rule (annotate); 5) Revoke keys if needed; 6) Collect evidence and mark incident for postmortem.
mitigation_playbook_details: Emergency throttle values suggested: 50rps per IP, 10rps per key, 5 concurrent streams per key for streaming endpoints. WAF rule TTL default 60m. Revocation flow must notify CS and issue replacement key. All emergency actions must be timeboxed and logged in the incident channel.
monitoring_and_alerting: Add alert: top-5-key-skew > 40% in 10m; add alert: sudden increase in WAF rule hits >200% baseline; dashboard: key usage, per-route 95p latency, GPU queue lengths, error budget burn rate.
postmortem_actions: Write postmortem in Confluence using template; attach logs and WAF hits; assign owners for short/medium/long term items; schedule tabletop to validate changes.
open_questions: What default throttle values should we set for hosted vs dedicated customers?; Should we create a policy for notifying customers when keys are revoked automatically?; How to instrument SDKs to avoid accidental public key leakage?
